title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM REHOBOAM'S PRIDE
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM REHOBOAM'S PRIDE
By Gospel Warrior
There are sins that destroy a man overnight.
And then there are sins that destroy generations.
Rehoboam taught me the difference.
His story is not merely about a king who made a bad decision.
It is about what happens when pride becomes louder than wisdom.
It is about what happens when power becomes more important than people.
It is about what happens when a man confuses authority with greatness.
And if we're honest, many of us have done the same.
Not from a throne.
But from a living room.
A workplace.
A marriage.
A ministry.
A friendship.
A social media account.
A position we thought made us somebody.
Rehoboam's story begins with extraordinary opportunity.
He was the son of King Solomon.
The heir of Israel's golden age.
The inheritor of unimaginable wealth, influence, prestige, and power.
Most people spend their entire lives trying to obtain what Rehoboam received simply by being born.
Yet one generation later, much of it would be gone.
Not because of military defeat.
Not because of famine.
Not because of foreign invasion.
Because of pride.
The biblical account is found primarily in 1 Kings 12 and 2 Chronicles 10.
The people of Israel came before their new king with a simple request.
They were exhausted.
Solomon's massive building projects had required heavy labor and taxation.
They pleaded for relief.
Scripture records their words:
"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."
(1 Kings 12:4)
The word translated "yoke" comes from the Hebrew word עֹל (ol).
A yoke was the wooden beam placed upon animals for labor.
The people were essentially saying:
"We are tired."
"We are burdened."
"We are carrying more than we can bear."
And they were willing to remain loyal if their king would simply listen.
Rehoboam had an opportunity every leader receives at some point.
The opportunity to choose humility over ego.
Listening over posturing.
Wisdom over insecurity.
For a moment, it looked like he might.
He sought counsel from the older men who had served his father Solomon.
These were experienced advisors.
Men who understood leadership.
Men who had witnessed both success and failure.
Their advice was remarkably simple.
"If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them and grant them their petition, then they will be your servants forever."
(1 Kings 12:7)
Notice the wisdom.
A king securing loyalty by becoming a servant.
Power through humility.
Strength through compassion.
Authority through service.
This principle would later be perfectly embodied by Jesus Christ Himself.
The Son of God declared:
"The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve."
The Greek word used there is διακονέω (diakoneō).
It means to minister, to serve, to attend to the needs of another.
The Kingdom of God has always operated upside down compared to the kingdoms of men.
Men seek greatness through domination.
God establishes greatness through servanthood.
Rehoboam was standing at a crossroads.
One road led toward unity.
The other toward division.
One road required humility.
The other required pride.
And pride often sounds younger than wisdom.
Louder than wisdom.
More exciting than wisdom.
More flattering than wisdom.
So Rehoboam dismissed the elders.
He turned instead to the young men who had grown up with him.
Men who told him exactly what his pride wanted to hear.
Men who mistook harshness for strength.
Cruelty for leadership.
Intimidation for authority.
Their advice became one of the most disastrous speeches in biblical history.
"My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs."
In modern language:
"You think my father was tough?
You haven't seen anything yet."
Then came the statement that shattered a kingdom.
"My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."
The result was immediate.
Ten tribes rebelled.
The kingdom split.
Civil conflict emerged.
Generations suffered.
A nation fractured.
All because one man chose pride over wisdom.
I used to read that story and wonder how anyone could be so foolish.
Then life humbled me.
Because Rehoboam is not merely a king from ancient history.
Rehoboam lives inside every human heart.
Every time we refuse correction.
Every time we become defensive when confronted.
Every time we value being right more than being reconciled.
Every time we surround ourselves only with people who agree with us.
Every time we reject wise counsel because it wounds our ego.
Every time we confuse confidence with arrogance.
We are standing exactly where Rehoboam stood.
The deeper lesson is hidden in the Hebrew understanding of pride itself.
One of the biblical words often associated with pride is גָּבַהּ (gavah).
It carries the idea of being high, elevated, exalted, lifted above.
The problem is not elevation itself.
God raises people.
God promotes people.
God blesses people.
The danger begins when the heart rises higher than its dependence upon God.
That is why Proverbs warns:
"Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall."
(Proverbs 16:18)
The fall begins long before the collapse becomes visible.
It starts internally.
In secret conversations with ourselves.
When we stop listening.
When we stop learning.
When we stop repenting.
When we stop being teachable.
Rehoboam's greatest tragedy was not losing territory.
It was losing the ability to hear wisdom.
A person who cannot be corrected is already in danger.
A person who cannot be challenged is already drifting.
A person who cannot admit fault is already becoming isolated.
The older I get, the more I realize that wisdom rarely flatters.
Wisdom often hurts first.
Healing comes later.
Correction feels uncomfortable.
But destruction is far more painful.
What amazes me most is how different Jesus was.
Jesus possessed infinitely more authority than Rehoboam.
Yet He never used power to elevate Himself.
The Apostle Paul describes Christ with breathtaking words.
The Greek text says He "ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτόν" (ekenōsen heauton).
"He emptied Himself."
(Philippians 2:7)
The King of kings chose humility.
The Creator washed feet.
The Lord became a servant.
The Judge carried a cross.
The One who deserved a crown first accepted thorns.
Rehoboam teaches us what pride destroys.
Jesus shows us what humility restores.
One divided a kingdom.
The other built an eternal Kingdom.
One demanded service.
The other became a servant.
One elevated himself and lost people.
The other humbled Himself and saved people.
That contrast changed the way I read Rehoboam forever.
Because the lesson was never merely about an ancient king.
It was about me.
Maybe it's about you too.
Maybe there is a conversation you've been avoiding because pride refuses to apologize.
Maybe there is wisdom you've been resisting because correction feels uncomfortable.
Maybe there is a relationship being strained because being right matters more than being reconciled.
Maybe God is trying to speak through voices you've already dismissed.
Be honest.
Have you become harder to correct lately?
Have you surrounded yourself only with people who tell you what you want to hear?
Have you confused strength with stubbornness?
Have you mistaken authority for maturity?
Rehoboam lost a kingdom in a moment.
Most people lose theirs slowly.
One decision at a time.
One act of pride at a time.
One ignored warning at a time.
One rejected correction at a time.
And then one day they look around and wonder why everything feels fractured.
The lesson I learned from Rehoboam's pride is painfully simple.
The greatest threat to my future is not what others might do to me.
It is what pride might do within me.
The people who change history are rarely the loudest people in the room.
They are often the most teachable.
The most humble.
The quickest to repent.
The quickest to listen.
The quickest to kneel before God.
And perhaps that is why Scripture repeatedly reminds us:
"God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
(James 4:6)
The Greek word for humble is ταπεινός (tapeinos).
It describes one who willingly lowers himself before God.
Not weak.
Not worthless.
Not insignificant.
Simply aware of who God is and who they are.
That awareness changes everything.
Because humility is not thinking less of yourself.
It is thinking of yourself less and Christ more.
And pride never looks uglier than when it stands next to the humility of Jesus.
Maybe that's why Rehoboam still matters.
His story warns us before we repeat it.
His failure teaches us before we experience it.
His pride becomes a mirror.
And what we do after looking into that mirror may determine far more than we realize.
Be honest. This hit harder than some of us expected.
Many believers fight this war repeatedly.
The kingdom Rehoboam lost began in his heart long before it disappeared from his hands.
